title: Checkpoint: Hard Moral Choices
objective: After this level you can reason through a new moral dilemma with at least two moral theories and say where they agree and split.
summary: Run through Transplant, the theories mostly agree the surgeon must not operate but split on why, while a few utilitarians bite the bullet.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: one new dilemma, several ways to reason.
cards.body: You’ve met the trolley, the pond and the murderer at the door. Now take a case you haven’t seen, and run the theories through it.

cards.headline: A new case: Transplant
cards.body: Foot and Thomson also discussed a hospital case. Five patients will die without transplants, each needing a different organ. A healthy visitor, in for routine tests, is a match for all five. A surgeon could save the five by taking his organs, but it would end his life. Five for one, once more.

cards.headline: Three ways to reason about Transplant

items.label: Count the outcomes
points: Classical utilitarianism seems to say operate
Most people find that result abominable

items.label: Revise the count
points: Some count a killing as worse than a death

items.label: Doing and intending
points: Foot: killing one is not letting five die
Double effect: harm as a means is ruled out

cards.headline: Agree on what, split on why
cards.body: Line them up and a pattern appears. Most views reach the same verdict, don’t operate, but for different reasons: the donor’s rights, a killing counted as worse than a death, or the line between killing and letting die. The sharpest split is with utilitarians who bite the bullet, arguing that such unrealistic cases shouldn’t be trusted to our intuitions.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: How to run a new dilemma through consequences, rights and the line between killing and letting die.
Why many who would pull the switch refuse to push, and how double effect tries to explain it.
What Singer’s pond, Bentham’s question and Parfit’s depletion case say we owe to others.
Why Kant wouldn’t lie to a murderer, and how luck muddies blame for two careless drivers.

questions.prompt: Hard Moral Choices recap: which case did Foot set beside her runaway tram?

options.label: A doctor choosing which of two patients to treat first
A judge who could stop rioters by framing one innocent man
A ship’s captain throwing cargo overboard in a storm
A child drowning in a shallow pond

questions.explanation: Foot paired the tram with a judge who could stop rioters from killing five only by framing one innocent man.

questions.prompt: Hard Moral Choices recap: what did Singer’s principle of equal consideration give equal weight to?

options.label: The like interests of all affected, whatever their species
The interests of human beings, and only theirs
The interests of the most intelligent beings
The wishes of the majority of those affected
options.rationale: It is about interests, not votes.

questions.explanation: Singer’s principle gives equal weight to the like interests of all those affected by our actions.

questions.prompt: In Hard Moral Choices, why do some consequentialists say the surgeon in Transplant must not operate?

options.label: They think the five patients matter less
options.rationale: The count of patients doesn’t change.

options.label: They follow Kant’s rule against lying
options.rationale: That is a different theory and a different duty.

options.label: They say the visitor gave consent
options.rationale: The case says nothing of consent.

options.label: They count a killing as worse than a death

questions.explanation: Some consequentialists revise their theory of value so that one killing counts as worse than five deaths that are not killings, which brings them to “don’t operate”.

questions.prompt: Hard Moral Choices recap: why does Parfit’s depletion choice seem to make no future person worse off?

options.label: It raises everyone’s quality of life for all time to come
options.rationale: Life gets much lower after two centuries.

options.label: It changes who is conceived, so they wouldn’t otherwise exist
Future people are not affected by how resources are used
The community asked future people for permission

questions.explanation: Depletion changes who gets conceived, so the later people would never have existed under conservation.

questions.prompt: Hard Moral Choices recap: which pair correctly contrasts the Mohists, Level 6’s critics of lavish funerals, with the Confucian Mencius?

options.label: Mohists: family comes first; Mencius: care for all people equally
Both: only rulers need to care for others
Mohists: inclusive care for all; Mencius: care growing out from the family
Mohists: follow ritual strictly; Mencius: abandon ritual altogether
options.rationale: Their dispute here is about whom to care for.

questions.explanation: The Mohists argued for inclusive care without distinctions; Mencius defended care with distinctions, extending love outward from the family.
